sentences.text: The eastern moa is the sole species recognized in the genus Emeus, a group established by Reichenbach in 1852. This bird belongs to the class Aves, the order Dinornithiformes, and the family Dinornithidae.

Standing approximately 1.5 meters tall, the animal weighed between 36 and 79 kilograms. It possessed a long neck, large powerful legs with short strong tarsi, and beige hair-like feathers without vestigial wing bones.

The tarsometatarsus of the eastern moa was restricted to motion in the parasagittal plane, similar to most other ratites. The pelvic musculature was poorly adapted for running, and the exceptionally wide feet compared to other moa species made it a very slow creature.
The eggs of the eastern moa measured 17.9 by 13.4 centimeters and weighed 1.9 kilograms.
Analysis of DNA from bone material confirmed that females of E. crassus were 15-25% larger than males.

Richard Owen originally described the first specimens of this animal in 1846, initially placing them in the genus Dinornis. Remains originally classified as Dinornis were later reclassified into the distinct genus Emeus.
The eastern moa lived exclusively on the South Island of New Zealand, inhabiting lowland forests, grasslands, dunelands, and shrublands.
During the Last Glacial Maximum, the eastern moa was confined to a single glacial refugium before its range expanded during the Holocene.
The eastern moa species went extinct around the year 1400. The fossil range of the genus Emeus spans from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, approximately 0.129 to 0 million years ago.
Researchers have long suspected that previously described species Emeus huttonii and E. crassus were actually male and female variants of a single species.
